title: The Art of War
author: Sun Tzu
openingText: The art of war is of vital importance to the State. It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin. Hence it is a subject of inquiry which can on no account be neglected. The art of war, then, is governed by five constant factors, to be taken into account in one's deliberations, when seeking to determine the conditions obtaining in the field.
about: Thirteen short chapters written 2,500 years ago by a Chinese general. The entire argument is this: winning by fighting is expensive and uncertain; winning without fighting is the highest skill. Every principle follows from that.

angleCards.title: Winning without fighting.
angleCards.text: Sun Tzu's central claim is that the supreme victory is the one achieved without battle. I want to follow that principle through all thirteen chapters and understand what it demands of a commander — in terms of preparation, intelligence, and patience.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Art of War as a philosophy of minimum force — the idea that the best general wins without fighting, and what that principle actually means in practice.

angleCards.title: War as a psychological contest.
angleCards.text: Sun Tzu is less interested in weapons than in morale, deception, and information. I want to track how consistently he treats the outcome of battles as already decided by psychological conditions — and whether that holds up against history.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read The Art of War as an argument that all conflict is psychological before it is physical — that what happens in the minds of commanders and troops determines the outcome before anyone draws a weapon.

angleCards.title: Beyond the battlefield.
angleCards.text: The book has been applied to business strategy, sports, and personal decision-making for decades. I want to read it with those applications in mind — not to flatten the military context, but to find where the principles genuinely generalise and where the analogy breaks.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to apply the principles outside their military context — to negotiation, business, or personal decisions — and test which ones actually translate.

angleCards.title: Self-knowledge as strategy.
angleCards.text: "Know your enemy and know yourself and you need not fear the result of a hundred battles." I want to take that claim seriously — what does it mean to truly know yourself in a conflict, and what does Sun Tzu say it requires?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand what Sun Tzu means by "know your enemy and know yourself" — what it actually requires to achieve that, and why he considers it the foundation of everything else.

cast.name: Sun Tzu
cast.description: Chinese general and military theorist writing around 500 BCE. The text is both a practical manual and a philosophical treatise — he is not describing what generals do, but what the ideal general would do.

cast.name: The General
cast.description: A composite figure described throughout — calm, adaptable, informed, and capable of holding the full complexity of a campaign in mind at once. Not a hero but an instrument of precision.

cast.name: The Sovereign
cast.description: The political authority who must be kept at a distance from tactical decisions. Sun Tzu is explicit: a ruler who interferes in the general's domain out of pride or impatience will lose. Authority and expertise must stay in their proper lanes.

cast.name: The Enemy
cast.description: Not to be hated or underestimated — to be understood. Sun Tzu treats the enemy as a system to be read: their morale, their supply lines, their commanders' temperament. Contempt is a liability; knowledge is the advantage.

cast.name: The Terrain
cast.description: Sun Tzu devotes entire chapters to ground: narrow passes, open plains, flooded ground, high positions. The terrain is not passive — it shapes what is possible and impossible, and the general who ignores it has already lost.

cast.name: The Spy
cast.description: The final chapter, and in some ways the most important. Sun Tzu argues that intelligence — knowing what the enemy plans before they act — is the one factor that makes all the other principles possible. Without it, strategy is guesswork.
